summary: Reports on a workshop sponsored by the Internet Research Steering Group on very high speed networks. It is for information only.

eli5.summary: Researchers met to talk about networks that move huge amounts of data very quickly, and this is a write-up of their talks.

questions: irsg workshop on very high speed networks
subtitle: Research insights on protocols, applications, and technologies for gigabit-speed networks

tldr.problem: As fiber optics promised terabit-speed capabilities, the research community needed to understand what changes to protocols, applications, and network hardware would be required to achieve and use gigabit-per-second networks effectively.
tldr.mechanism: The Internet Research Steering Group convened a workshop of fifty leading researchers across eight sessions covering protocol implementation, high-speed applications, lightwave technology, ATM and phone system integration, distributed systems, host interfaces, congestion control, and switch architectures. Experts presented current work and identified open research challenges.
tldr.outcome: The workshop identified that gigabit networks would require fundamental rethinking of RPC, resource reservation, host-network interfaces, and congestion control, while emerging technologies like ATM and photonic networking showed promise for future infrastructure.

today: RFC 1152 is an Informational report documenting research discussions from April 1990. Many of the challenges identified—scaling RPC, network interface design, ATM deployment, multicast applications—continue to influence network research today, while some predictions (like the end of off-board protocol processors) proved prescient. The document is a valuable snapshot of the research community's thinking on the eve of the commercial gigabit networking era.

sections.title: Workshop Overview and Scope
sections.content:
In April 1990, the Internet Research Steering Group (IRSG) hosted a workshop bringing together fifty of the world's leading high-speed network researchers. The goal was to stimulate innovative thinking about research challenges posed by emerging gigabit-speed networking technology. Attendance was selective—applications were reviewed and about half were accepted—with a few key researchers invited directly by the program committee. Organized by Dave Clark and Craig Partridge, the workshop distilled discussions across eight sessions into a report reflecting the collective insights of the community.

The workshop examined not just speed itself, but the broader requirements: long-distance operation, support for many users, new services like bandwidth reservation, and integration with emerging applications in multimedia and scientific visualization.
sections.eli5: The top researchers in the country met for a few days to figure out what was hard about making networks really fast and how to solve those problems.

sections.title: Protocols, Implementation, and Resource Reservation
sections.content:
David Clark opened the protocol session by asserting that existing protocols like TCP and IP could theoretically operate at gigabit speeds if that were the only goal. However, practical deployment would require resource reservation (guaranteeing bandwidth for specific applications), long-distance links, and support for many simultaneous users. Van Jacobson reported that experimentally, existing connectionless protocols like IP could support resource reservation without requiring connection setup, challenging the conventional wisdom. Dave Borman described running TCP on a Cray supercomputer at over 500 Mbps, suggesting protocol overhead was manageable if hardware was fast enough.

Dave Feldmeier described the Aurora project's development of a 1 Gbps transport protocol with forward error correction chips to handle ATM cell loss. The consensus was that protocols would need careful design for high speeds, but existing approaches could be adapted rather than requiring entirely new protocols.
sections.eli5: The network rules (protocols) might not need to change much to be fast. The real tricks were reservation of bandwidth, handling long distances, and making the computers fast enough.

sections.title: Application Requirements and Multimedia Collaboration
sections.content:
Keith Lantz introduced the concept of the 'portable office'—a world where workers could access the same services and people regardless of physical location, using high-bandwidth multimedia. Desktop teleconferencing emerged as a killer application, requiring real-time audio and video with low latency and minimal jitter, plus synchronization of multiple data streams. Charlie Catlett analyzed scientific applications, specifically thunderstorm simulation: simulation on a Cray created data at 32–128 Mbps, tessellation output at 10–100 Mbps, and a Silicon Graphics workstation rendered 100,000 polygons per second. Future projections included simulation rates reaching several gigabits per second as supercomputers and workstations increased in power.

Terry Crowley expanded the theme to include shared multimedia workspaces, video mail, distributed file systems, and network access to scientific visualization. Greg Watson at Hewlett-Packard argued that while supercomputers drive technology, moderate-bandwidth applications (around 10 Mbps per workstation) would drive economic adoption. The key challenge was supporting multiple synchronized data streams and multicast delivery to multiple sites simultaneously.
sections.eli5: People wanted to work together from far away with video and pictures, and scientists needed huge files from supercomputers. This meant the network had to move a lot of different types of data all at the same time.

sections.title: Fiber Optics, ATM, and Network Architectures
sections.content:
Bob Kennedy proposed all-optical networks exploiting the tens of terahertz bandwidth available in fiber, with optoelectronic nodes recognizing and routing only traffic destined for them. Rich Gitlin described a three-level broadband architecture using B-ISDN/ATM at 150 Mbps, with ATM switches as the core and SONET circuits providing reconfigurable digital cross-connects. The planned LuckyNet at Bell Labs would provide gigabit-per-second capability to heterogeneous users, with video conferencing and LAN interconnection as initial applications.

Wally St. John's Los Alamos gigabit testbed used High-Performance Parallel Interface (HPPI) crossbar switches operating at 800–1600 Mbps. A key challenge was mapping HPPI packets to SONET frames while managing flow control and error rates. Researchers discussed whether ATM backbones should be used only for transmission or also for switching, and whether static or dynamic routing would be best for short-lived connections.
sections.eli5: Fiber optic cables could carry huge amounts of data. New technologies like ATM and SONET let networks switch and combine these huge flows. Researchers were building test networks to see what worked best.

sections.title: Distributed Systems and the RPC Problem
sections.content:
Craig Partridge highlighted a fundamental challenge: in gigabit networks, classical Remote Procedure Call (RPC) would not scale well because network round-trip delay remains roughly constant due to the speed of light, while processors become exponentially faster. This means the cost of waiting for an RPC reply grows from thousands of instruction cycles to millions. Futures and parallel RPC do not fully solve this. Instead, consolidating multiple RPC requests into larger transactions run on the remote machine might work better. Dave Cheriton argued that in gigabit networks, the network becomes the primary resource and should be managed by the operating system. Jonathan Smith countered that caching and anticipation could work if designed carefully, citing the cost of an additional page fetch (32 microseconds) versus missing and having to request it again (5 milliseconds).

Research on distributed virtual memory, asynchronous programming paradigms with causal consistency, and new RPC designs all emerged as necessary areas of investigation. The challenge was that fundamental assumptions about distributed systems—synchronous communication, blocking calls—no longer fit gigabit-speed reality.
sections.eli5: Programs that asked remote computers for things would be waiting forever because light is slow compared to fast computers. Researchers had to figure out new ways for programs to work together without waiting.

sections.title: Host Interfaces and the Memory-Bus Bottleneck
sections.content:
Gary Delp and others discussed the challenges of connecting hosts to gigabit networks. Key issues included media access, compression, forward error correction, encryption, memory mapping, and presentation layer overhead. Jeff Mogul observed that in a hypothetical late-1990s workstation with a 1000-MIPS CPU and gigabit LAN, the bottleneck would not be protocol processing but the cost of moving data into the CPU cache and notifying processes—potentially hundreds of instruction cycles just for the first cache miss. Off-board protocol processors would become useless; instead, memory-mapped network interfaces visible to the host processor might be ideal.

Specific implementations showed trade-offs: Nectar at Carnegie Mellon used communication processor boards (CABs) that off-loaded protocol processing, achieving 70 Mbps between processors on the CABs but only 25 Mbps between host processes due to VME interface bottlenecks. The Los Alamos HPPI testbed used VLSI crossbar designs capable of 25 Mbps to 1 Gbps. Research on DMA, large packets, and large channel transfer requests suggested that direct memory access and bulk operations—not per-packet interrupts—would be key to high-speed host-network integration.
sections.eli5: Connecting computers to gigabit networks was tricky because moving data into memory and telling the program about it costs many CPU cycles. Different approaches (separate protocol chips, memory mapping, DMA) each had pros and cons.

viz.caption: Distributed Systems Challenges at Gigabit Speeds

items.title: Network Latency
items.text: Round-trip delay cannot improve below the speed of light; CPU speeds continue rising, making waiting increasingly expensive.

items.title: Synchronization
items.text: Consistency and concurrency control become harder in distributed systems with non-deterministic timing.

items.title: RPC Design
items.text: Classical RPC patterns break; alternatives like transaction consolidation and anticipatory caching are needed.

items.title: Service Scalability
items.text: System services must scale to larger user communities without performance degradation per user.
